prime.problem: A 124M-parameter model can train for hours with a silent bug (gradients never cleared, targets not shifted, a step that updates nothing) and the loss will still wobble downwards a little. You need a fast yes-or-no test that the whole training step works, and then a way to feed the model new text every step.
prime.fits: The first-loss card gave you a batch x, y and a loss of 10.96 at init. This card adds the optimizer loop that makes that number fall, the same overfit-one-batch check you did in the MLP course, and the loader that the rest of the lecture grows into sharded, multi-GPU loading.
expect: overfitting one batch as a test
prime.goal: Write the training loop and the loader yourself, use the one-batch test to prove the loop works, and explain why real-data loss stalls near 6.3 after 50 steps instead of falling to 0.

attend: Why is a loss near 0 on one repeated batch evidence that the step works, and not evidence that the model is good?
Which of the four lines does the init-loss check (10.96 vs 10.82) leave untested, and which does the one-batch run test?
What does the model learn first on new text, and what number does that alone get you to on tiny shakespeare?
How does next_batch make y the next token of x without building a separate target array?
When exactly does the loader wrap to position 0, and why are the last 105 tokens never used?

must: One fixed batch = only 128 answers to fit → 124M parameters can memorise them → loss falls towards 0 (0.36 at step 49) → if it doesn't, something in the forward, backward or optimizer step is broken

A new batch each step → the model can't memorise what it hasn't seen → the quickest thing to learn is how common each token is → the loss heads for the frequency-only entropy (6.32 here) before context starts to help
backward adds into .grad → without zero_grad each step would also carry every earlier step's gradients → the update is wrong even though the loss is computed correctly

Walk the token row in B·T chunks, take B·T + 1 tokens → x = buf[:-1], y = buf[1:] are shifted by one → every position gets its next-token target for free → one integer of state covers each token once per epoch
elevated: The printed loss in run B is measured on that step's own batch → it wobbles (6.95 at step 29, 7.53 at step 39) → never read one step's loss as a trend; the validation loss later averages over many batches
reference: the final sharded loader in train_gpt2.py L214–L252 adds process_rank, num_processes and shard files
loss.item() copies the scalar back to the CPU for printing

compress.prompt: From memory, write the four lines of a training step and label what each one does. Then in 3–4 sentences explain why run A reaches 0.36 and run B stops near 6.8, and sketch how next_batch cuts x and y out of the token row.
checklist: one repeated batch can be memorised, so its loss falls towards 0; that proves the plumbing
new batches can't be memorised; token frequencies are learned first
frequency-only loss = entropy of the token distribution = 6.32, vs 10.82 for a uniform guess
the loader takes B·T + 1 tokens; x drops the last, y drops the first
the position advances by B·T and wraps to 0 when the next window won't fit

retrieve.q: Explain why overfitting a single batch is a useful test for a training script even though an overfit model is useless.
answer: a working model with a working step must be able to memorise 128 targets
so a loss that won't fall points to a bug, not to a hard problem
it runs in under a minute, unlike a real training run
memorising says nothing about generalisation; that is measured on held-out data

retrieve.q: Walk through two calls of next_batch with B=4, T=32 starting from position 0: which token indices go into buf, x and y each time, and what is the position afterwards?
answer: call 1: buf = tokens 0–128 (129 ids); x = 0–127, y = 1–128, both viewed as (4, 32)
position becomes 128
position becomes 256; it wraps to 0 only when position + 129 would run past 338,025

retrieve.q: Run B ends at 6.80 after 50 steps. Is that a sign something is wrong? What reference numbers would you compare it with, and what would a stubborn 10.8 or an instant 0.4 each suggest?
answer: no: 6.80 is between the uniform guess (10.82) and the frequency-only floor (6.32), as expected for 50 steps
stuck near 10.8: the step isn't updating (missing step, lr 0, gradients not flowing)
near 0 on new data this fast: the data is leaking or repeating, e.g. the loader returns the same batch
a single step's value is noisy, so look at several

retrieve.q: Why does the lecture's loader walk the text in order instead of drawing random offsets like the GPT lecture's get_batch? What do you give up?
answer: in order: each token is used once per epoch, and the state is one integer
it extends cleanly to shards and to splitting positions across GPUs by rank
you give up shuffling: batches arrive in document order, a caveat noted in the results

compare.q: The MLP course overfit 32 examples with a small net; here GPT-2 overfits 128 tokens. What is the same about the test, and what does the much larger model change about how fast and how far the loss drops?
answer: same logic: many parameters, few examples → the loss should head towards 0, or there's a bug
the same caveat: memorising proves the loop, not the model
GPT-2 has 124M parameters for 128 targets, so it memorises quickly (0.36 in 50 steps) with AdamW
neither reaches exactly 0 when some identical inputs need different targets

compare.q: The GPT lecture sampled random chunk starts with torch.randint; DataLoaderLite walks the text in order. What is fundamentally different, which design choice causes it, and when does each one fail?
answer: random offsets: overlapping windows, no epochs, some tokens seen twice and others never in a given number of steps
in order: disjoint windows, exact epochs, deterministic
the cause is the state: a random draw per batch vs one advancing position
random fails to give clean epoch accounting; in-order fails to shuffle, so ordered data can bias training

compare.q: Run A's loss is 0.36 and run B's is 6.80. Which one is closer to what a validation loss would report for each model, and why?
answer: run A's model would score badly on held-out text: 0.36 is on the batch it memorised
run B's per-batch loss is on text it hadn't seen yet, so it already behaves like a validation measurement
validation loss averages many held-out batches to remove the step-to-step noise

predict.q: Keep run B going for 300 steps instead of 50 (still under one epoch). Will its per-batch loss drop below the 6.32 frequency-only floor, and what would it mean if it stayed pinned at 6.32?
predict.answer: It drops below. Run for this card with labs/overfit-then-load.py --steps 300, most batches from step 189 on score between 4.5 and 6.0 (e.g. 4.5151 at step 219, 4.9210 at step 289), though single batches still spike (6.3880 at step 299). Going below 6.32 is only possible by using the tokens before. A loss pinned at 6.32 would mean the model is ignoring context, so suspect the attention, the positions or the x/y shift.

apply.task: Compute the frequency-only loss yourself. Tokenize tiny shakespeare with tiktoken gpt2, count every token id, turn the counts into shares p, and compute −Σ p ln p. Also count how many distinct token ids appear and how many of the 50,257 never do.
apply.done: You get 338,025 tokens, 11,706 distinct ids (38,551 never used), '\n' as the most common token with 39,996 occurrences, and an entropy of 6.3161.
apply.hint: collections.Counter(tokens) gives the counts; divide each by len(tokens).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: run A's 0.36, run B's 6.80, or whether 300 steps gets below 6.32?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why memorising proves the step works, or why frequencies come before context?
